guide.title: Steakhouses in San Francisco: Eleven Rooms and a Van Ness Spine
guide.intro: Eleven rooms on this page, all of them inside the city, and no South Bay page pulling the mass south the way Korean barbecue's did. Three sit on one avenue: Harris' at Van Ness and Pacific, the House of Prime Rib two blocks down at Washington, Ruth's Chris further south at California Street. Three more take the Financial District and the waterfront — the Vault inside a bank vault at 555 California, 5A5 on Jackson Street, Epic Steak on the Embarcadero facing the Bay Bridge. The rest are scattered by genre rather than by street: an Argentine asador in the Mission, a churrascaria on Market Street, a second one in SoMa, a Michelin-starred wagyu room on Division Street, and a surf-and-turf house on Lombard. Three Union Square rooms are published on the Union Square guide and linked below.

sections.heading: The Van Ness spine
sections.body:
Three rooms on six blocks of one avenue, and they are the closest thing this city has to a steakhouse row.

Harris' Restaurant holds the corner of Van Ness and Pacific, with a dry-aging cooler set into the storefront window so the beef is the first thing you see from the sidewalk. Ann Lee Harris opened it in 1984 in the old Grison's Steakhouse space, according to the restaurant's own history, and Michael Buhagiar has been sole owner since 2018.

Two blocks south at 1906 Van Ness, the House of Prime Rib carves roasts at the table from stainless carts, to whatever thickness you ask for. Joe Betz bought the restaurant in 1985 and ran it for four decades; he died in 2025 at eighty-six, and the room he built is still the one on the avenue people queue for.

Ruth's Chris takes the southern end at 1601 Van Ness, the city's outpost of the national chophouse chain.

sections.heading: The Financial District and the Embarcadero
sections.body:
Three rooms east of the hill, one of them literally inside a bank.

The Vault Steakhouse opened in October 2025 on the concourse level of 555 California Street, in the original bank vault of the building, with chefs Ryan Cerizo and Jason Halverson running it and a piano playing every night. 5A5 Steak Lounge is a few blocks north on Jackson Street in Jackson Square, working Japanese A5 wagyu — the grade the room is named for.

Epic Steak sits on the water at 369 The Embarcadero, a dining room turned to the Bay Bridge and Treasure Island. Executive chef Parke Ulrich came across from Waterbar next door and applies the same restraint to prime dry-aged beef that he did to fish.

sections.heading: The Marina, the Mission, Market Street and the Design District
sections.body:
Five rooms with no cluster between them, each one carrying a different genre.

Bobo's is on Lombard Street in the Marina, where dry-aged Prime steak shares the table with Pacific Dungeness crab and there is garaged parking underneath the room. Lolinda is on Mission Street at 21st, an Argentine asador whose wood-fired grill gives every cut its char; the house calls its prime bone-in ribeye for two the Guacho.

Espetus Churrascaria is at 1686 Market Street at Gough, where fourteen signature cuts come round on skewers grilled over mesquite charcoal and the rodízio keeps coming until you turn the card. Fogo de Chão runs the same service at 201 Third Street in SoMa, with a butcher shop selling ready-to-grill cuts on the way out.

Niku Steakhouse is on Division Street in the Design District and holds a Michelin star. It dry-ages in house at an adjoining butchery, serves Japanese A5 and American wagyu, and seats eighteen at a chef's counter over the coals under executive chef Dustin Falcon.

sections.heading: Union Square, published on its own guide
sections.body:
Three of the city's fifteen steakhouse rooms stand within four blocks of Union Square, and all three already have place pages on the Union Square neighborhood guide.

Morton's The Steakhouse is at 400 Post Street, Alexander's Steakhouse at 165 O'Farrell Street with its wagyu program, and ABSteak by Akira Back at 124 Ellis Street, a Korean-inflected steakhouse that qualifies here on the same ground as any other beef room. A room is published once on this site, so this page names them and links to the guide that carries them.

Alfred's Steakhouse is a different room from Alexander's and is not on this page: its trading status could not be confirmed, and an unconfirmed room is left off rather than hedged.

faq.question: What makes a room a steakhouse on this page?
faq.answer: Steak has to be the menu's center of gravity, plus the beef-centric genres — churrascaria, Argentine parrilla, Japanese wagyu counter, Korean-style beef room. That admits Espetus and Fogo de Chão, Lolinda's asador, and the wagyu rooms at Niku and 5A5. It also decides what stays off: the Brazen Head in Cow Hollow is a continental public house with escargot, French onion soup and one signature pepper steak, which is a restaurant that serves a good steak rather than a steakhouse.

faq.question: Why are Morton's, Alexander's and ABSteak not listed as rooms here?
faq.answer: All three qualify, and all three already have place pages on the Union Square guide. A room is published once on this site, so this page names them in prose and links to the guide that carries them. That is three of the city's fifteen rooms accounted for elsewhere, which is why eleven are published here.

faq.question: Is Alfred's Steakhouse the same room as Alexander's?
faq.answer: No. They are two different restaurants with similar names, and the survey checked them separately. Alexander's Steakhouse is counted and published on the Union Square guide. Alfred's could not be confirmed as trading after 2020, so it is excluded outright rather than published with a hedge.

faq.question: Why is there no South Bay or Peninsula section?
faq.answer: Because the city holds the count on its own. Fifteen rooms sit inside San Francisco, which is enough for a page without reaching down to Santa Clara or San Jose. That is the opposite of what the Korean barbecue survey found, where the South Bay pulled hard enough to need a page of its own.

faq.question: Which room is inside a bank vault?
faq.answer: The Vault Steakhouse, on the concourse level of 555 California Street. The dining room is the building's original bank vault, and the restaurant opened there in October 2025.

photos.title: Van Ness Avenue looking north at night
photos.description: A long-exposure night view down a wide avenue from several stories up, white headlight trails running away from the camera and red tail-light trails running toward it, street trees breaking the lanes, apartment blocks and low commercial buildings on both sides, and hills and construction cranes on the far skyline. Van Ness Avenue, looking north from 100 Van Ness.
photos.author: Dllu

places.name: Harris' Restaurant
places.address: 2100 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco, CA 94109
places.summary: Harris' holds the corner of Van Ness Avenue and Pacific, with a dry-aging cooler built into the storefront window so slabs of beef face the sidewalk. Inside it is dark wood, brass and leather booths.
places.history: Ann Lee Harris opened the room in 1984 in the former Grison's Steakhouse space, according to the restaurant's own history, with chef Goetz Boje and manager Joey Buhagiar; Michael Buhagiar became sole owner in 2018.

places.name: House of Prime Rib
places.address: 1906 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco, CA 94109
places.summary: The House of Prime Rib is a prime rib room on Van Ness Avenue at Washington Street. Roasts of beef are wheeled to the table on stainless carts and carved to the thickness you ask for.
places.history: Joe Betz bought the restaurant in 1985 and ran it for four decades; he died in 2025 at eighty-six.

places.name: Ruth's Chris Steak House
places.address: 1601 Van Ness Ave, San Francisco, CA 94109
places.summary: Ruth's Chris takes the southern end of the Van Ness steakhouse spine at California Street, the city's outpost of the national chophouse chain.

places.name: The Vault Steakhouse
places.address: 555 California St, Concourse Level, San Francisco, CA 94104
places.summary: The Vault Steakhouse sits on the concourse level of 555 California Street, in the original bank vault of the building. Chefs Ryan Cerizo and Jason Halverson run the steaks and a piano plays nightly.

places.name: 5A5 Steak Lounge
places.summary: 5A5 Steak Lounge is on Jackson Street in Jackson Square, and Japanese A5 wagyu is the grade the room is named for and built on.

places.name: EPIC Steak
places.summary: EPIC Steak stands on the waterfront at 369 The Embarcadero, its dining room turned to the Bay Bridge and Treasure Island. Prime dry-aged cuts are the menu, with seafood beside them; executive chef Parke Ulrich came from Waterbar next door.

places.name: Niku Steakhouse
places.summary: Niku Steakhouse is a one-star Michelin room on Division Street in the Design District, dry-aging its beef at an adjoining butchery and serving Japanese A5 and American wagyu. Eighteen seats face a chef's counter over the coals, where executive chef Dustin Falcon works the wood fire.

places.name: Bobo's
places.summary: Bobo's is a Lombard Street steakhouse in the Marina where dry-aged Prime beef meets Pacific Dungeness crab on the same menu. There is garaged parking underneath the restaurant.

places.name: Lolinda
places.summary: Lolinda is an Argentine steakhouse on Mission Street built on the wood-fired asador, the traditional Argentine grill that gives each cut its char. The house signature is the Guacho, a prime bone-in ribeye for two.

places.name: Espetus Churrascaria
places.summary: Espetus is a Brazilian churrascaria at Market Street and Gough, where gaúcho chefs grill skewered cuts over mesquite charcoal and carve them at the table. Fourteen signature cuts of beef, pork, chicken, lamb and shrimp come round in continuous rodízio service.

places.name: Fogo de Chão
places.address: 201 Third St, Suite 100, San Francisco, CA 94103
places.summary: Fogo de Chão's SoMa room is on Third Street, roasting cuts of beef over open flame in the churrasco tradition and carving them at the table. A Fogo butcher shop inside sells ready-to-grill cuts, and there is an outdoor patio.

entries.name: Harris' Restaurant
entries.note: Van Ness at Pacific. Look in the window before you go in — the aging cooler is the restaurant's front door argument.

entries.name: House of Prime Rib
entries.note: 1906 Van Ness Avenue. One dish, one cart, and a queue most nights.

entries.name: Ruth's Chris Steak House
entries.note: 1601 Van Ness Avenue. The southern anchor of the three-room Van Ness run.

entries.name: The Vault Steakhouse
entries.note: Concourse level, 555 California Street. You eat inside the building's original bank vault.

entries.name: 5A5 Steak Lounge
entries.note: Jackson Street, Jackson Square. The name is the beef grade, and the beef grade is the menu.

entries.name: EPIC Steak
entries.note: 369 The Embarcadero. Ask for the water side; the Bay Bridge fills the window.

entries.name: Niku Steakhouse
entries.note: Division Street, Design District. Eighteen counter seats over the coals, and a Michelin star above them.

entries.name: Bobo's
entries.note: Lombard Street, Marina. Surf and turf as a genuine proposition rather than a menu heading.

entries.name: Lolinda
entries.note: Mission Street at 21st. The asador is the point, and the Guacho is sized for two.

entries.name: Espetus Churrascaria
entries.note: Market Street at Gough. Fourteen cuts over mesquite, and the service does not stop until you say so.

entries.name: Fogo de Chão
entries.note: 201 Third Street, SoMa. The second churrascaria on the page, with a butcher counter inside it.

links.note: Morton's The Steakhouse at 400 Post Street, Alexander's Steakhouse at 165 O'Farrell Street and ABSteak by Akira Back at 124 Ellis Street all qualify under this collection's rule, but their place pages are published on the Union Square guide.
